did_you_know.text: Did you know? The phrase “we were like those who dream” describes how overwhelmed the people were when the LORD restored Zion’s fortunes; the change was so great that it seemed like a dream.

Did you know? This verse describes two expressions of joy: “our mouths were filled with laughter” and “our tongues with songs of joy.” The joy does not remain only in the heart; it is expressed in speech and song.

Did you know? According to the psalm, even the nations recognize the redemption and say, “The LORD has done great things for them.” In this way, the redemption is portrayed as an event visible to the whole world.

Did you know? The people respond to the nations’ words and repeat the phrase “The LORD has done great things,” but change “for them” to “for us,” adding, “We are glad.” This repetition emphasizes their personal recognition of the LORD’s goodness.
Did you know? After describing the joy of the past, the psalm turns to a request: “Restore our fortunes, LORD.” In this way, it moves from remembering redemption to praying for its completion.
Did you know? The return to Zion is compared to “streams in the Negev”—watercourses in a desert landscape. The image expresses a dramatic change from dryness and scarcity to flow and abundance.
Did you know? The verse presents a clear contrast between “tears” and “songs of joy”: those who sow in hardship and sorrow will eventually reap with joy.

Did you know? The sixth verse describes a complete process: a person goes out weeping, carrying seed, but returns with songs of joy, carrying sheaves. The seed symbolizes the fruits of labor that have ripened over time.
